segments.text: This is the hinge topic of the entire syllabus: it explains how a demand for constitutional safeguards within a united India (where Topic 4 left off, with the 1929 Fourteen Points) became, within roughly a decade, the demand for a separate sovereign state, and how that demand was actually achieved through a specific, contingent sequence of failed negotiations between 1940 and 1947. The most valuable habit for this topic is treating each mission or plan as a negotiation with three distinct parties — the Muslim League, the Congress, and the British — each with its own objective, and asking why each attempt at compromise specifically failed, rather than treating partition as an outcome that was somehow always going to happen.

blocks.text: Background: From Safeguards to a New Demand

segments.text: By the early 1930s, several developments had made the “safeguards within a united India” position (Topic 4) look increasingly fragile to a growing section of Muslim political opinion: the failure of the Nehru Report to satisfy Muslim demands, continuing communal tension following the Khilafat Movement’s collapse, and, most importantly, growing anxiety about what majority rule would actually mean in practice once real provincial self-government arrived under a future constitutional settlement. It is against this backdrop that Muhammad Iqbal, the philosopher-poet whose intellectual stature within Muslim political thought was second only to Jinnah’s political leadership, delivered his historically pivotal address at the annual Muslim League session at Allahabad.

In his presidential address to the Muslim League session at Allahabad in December 1930, Iqbal argued for the consolidation of Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Balochistan into a single, self-governing unit within the British Empire (or possibly, he suggested, outside it), as what he considered the “final destiny” of Muslims at least in north-western India. This is a genuinely important and easily misread text. Iqbal did not use the word “Pakistan” (which entered political usage only later, from around 1933, associated initially with a pamphlet by Choudhary Rahmat Ali proposing the name as an acronym), and he was addressing the specific constitutional debate of 1930 — anticipating what form of self-government north-western Muslim-majority India should have within the wider constitutional settlement then under discussion at the Round Table Conferences, not issuing a fully worked-out blueprint for a sovereign nation-state as it eventually emerged in 1947. Reading the address in its own 1930 constitutional context, rather than reducing it to a simple, modern-sounding one-line slogan about “the idea of Pakistan,” is essential for an accurate answer.

Three Round Table Conferences were held in London between 1930 and 1932, bringing together British officials and representatives of various Indian political and communal interests (Congress notably boycotted the first conference, participating only in the second, represented by Gandhi following the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 which had temporarily suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement) to negotiate the shape of the next constitutional reform. The conferences exposed, rather than resolved, deep disagreement over the fundamental shape of any future federal structure, over minority representation (leading eventually to the Communal Award discussed in Topic 3), and over the pace and extent of self-government — disagreement significant enough that the resulting Government of India Act 1935 (Topic 3) ultimately abandoned the fully worked federal scheme these conferences had debated, retaining only the provincial-autonomy provisions.

blocks.text: The 1935 Act, the 1937 Elections, and Congress Ministries

segments.text: Provincial elections held in 1937 under the newly implemented provincial-autonomy provisions of the 1935 Act produced a result of major long-term significance: the Indian National Congress won outright majorities or formed governments in a majority of provinces, while the Muslim League performed relatively poorly even in several Muslim-majority provinces, where regional Muslim parties (such as the Unionist Party in Punjab) often outperformed the League. The two-year period of Congress provincial government (1937–1939) that followed became
critically important to Muslim League politics

, not primarily because of any single policy, but because League leaders — and Jinnah in particular — argued that Congress ministries’ conduct (in matters such as the treatment of Urdu, the observance of Congress symbols and songs in schools, and what League propaganda characterised as insensitivity to Muslim religious and cultural concerns) demonstrated exactly the danger Sir Syed had warned of decades earlier: that Muslim interests would not be adequately protected under governments elected by, and primarily accountable to, a Hindu-majority electorate. Whether or not every specific complaint about the Congress ministries’ record was fully justified (historians differ on this point), the political effect was decisive: the League used this record extensively in a mass campaign to reposition itself, over the following years, as the sole authentic representative of Indian Muslims — directly setting up its later claim, from 1940 onward, to be the exclusive voice of Muslim political opinion.

Congress provincial ministries resigned in 1939 in protest at the Viceroy’s decision to declare India at war (as part of the British Empire) without any prior consultation of Indian political opinion — itself a further illustration of the underlying constitutional problem this whole topic addresses: how much genuine self-government had provincial autonomy actually delivered, if the empire’s most consequential decision (war) could still be made in London without Indian political consultation?
At its annual session in Lahore in March 1940, the Muslim League adopted what became known as the
Lahore Resolution

(sometimes later called, especially by opponents, the “Pakistan Resolution,” though that specific word does not appear in the resolution’s original text). The resolution demanded that geographically contiguous units in which Muslims were numerically in a majority — specifically identifying the north-western and eastern zones of British India — should be grouped to constitute
“independent States”

in which the constituent units would be autonomous and sovereign. This is a genuinely decisive turning point: for the first time, official Muslim League policy moved beyond safeguards within a united constitutional framework toward the explicit demand for separate, sovereign political units.

Two points deserve careful attention here, since they are frequently tested and frequently misunderstood. First, the original resolution’s wording refers to “States” in the plural, and later League interpretation and propaganda increasingly read this as pointing toward a single unified state called Pakistan, even though the exact relationship between the eastern and western Muslim-majority zones was left genuinely ambiguous in 1940 (an ambiguity that would resurface, with catastrophic consequences, in the geographic separation underlying the 1971 crisis covered in Topic 8). Second, as the historiographical debate discussed at the end of Topic 4 emphasises, adopting this resolution as formal League policy is not the same as Jinnah having irrevocably committed, from 1940 onward, to accepting nothing less than full sovereign partition — subsequent negotiations through 1946 show the League still willing, under the right conditions, to consider a looser federal arrangement for a united India, a point developed further below.

blocks.text: Wartime Negotiations: Cripps Mission, Quit India, and the Simla Conference

segments.text: The Cripps Mission (1942).

With Japanese forces advancing toward India’s eastern borders during the Second World War, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to offer a proposal for full dominion status after the war, together with a provision allowing any province to opt out of the proposed Indian union — a provision widely read as an implicit acknowledgment of the possibility of Pakistan, since it would have allowed Muslim-majority provinces to remain separate if they chose. The mission failed: Congress rejected the proposal chiefly because it offered no immediate transfer of power during the war itself, and the League regarded the proposed opt-out mechanism as insufficiently clear and guaranteed. Gandhi is reported to have described the offer as “a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank” — a memorable phrase capturing Congress’s core objection that the promise, however framed, was deferred beyond the point of practical trust.
Quit India (1942) and the Simla Conference (1945).

Congress’s subsequent Quit India Movement (already introduced in Topic 3) led to the mass arrest of virtually the entire Congress leadership for the remainder of the war, while the Muslim League, having largely stayed out of the movement, was able to consolidate and expand its own organisational strength relatively unimpeded during this period — an important, often overlooked factor in explaining the League’s markedly stronger electoral position by 1945–46 compared with 1937. As the war drew to a close, Viceroy Lord Wavell convened the
Simla Conference

in 1945, attempting to form a new, more representative interim central executive council with Indian members. The conference broke down primarily over Jinnah’s insistence that the Muslim League alone should have the exclusive right to nominate all Muslim members of the council — a claim Congress, which itself included Muslim members and rejected any single party’s exclusive claim to represent an entire religious community, refused to accept.

blocks.text: The 1945–46 Elections and the Cabinet Mission Plan

segments.text: Elections.

Provincial and central elections held in the winter of 1945–46 produced a result confirming the shift in Muslim political opinion since 1937: the Muslim League won an overwhelming majority of Muslim seats (though the precise translation of seats won into a claim to represent “all” Indian Muslims remains, again, a matter some historians treat more critically than others), substantially strengthening Jinnah’s claim to be the authoritative voice of Indian Muslim political opinion in subsequent negotiations.
The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946).

A British Cabinet delegation — the Cabinet Mission — arrived in 1946 with what many historians regard as the most serious and carefully constructed final attempt to preserve a united India while still addressing Muslim safeguard concerns. The plan proposed a three-tier structure: a weak central union government controlling only defence, foreign affairs and communications; provinces grouped into three sections (one predominantly Hindu-majority, and two predominantly Muslim-majority, covering the north-west and the Bengal-Assam region respectively) with the power to determine their own group-level constitutions; and a right for any province, after an initial period, to reconsider its position. Crucially, the plan proposed
no partition
of India — it sought to secure Muslim safeguards through provincial grouping and a weak centre rather than through separate sovereignty.

Both the League and Congress initially accepted the plan, but the agreement collapsed over a fundamental interpretive disagreement: Congress interpreted the provincial grouping provisions as optional for individual provinces (meaning a province could decline to join its assigned group), while the League interpreted the grouping as compulsory (an interpretation more consistent with the safeguards the League sought). When Congress leader Jawaharlal Nehru publicly stated, in July 1946, that Congress would enter the interim central government free to modify the plan’s provisions in the future through the constituent assembly process, the League concluded that Congress was not honouring the plan in the spirit intended and withdrew its own acceptance. The historian Ayesha Jalal’s argument (introduced in Topic 4) is particularly relevant here: she reads the Cabinet Mission Plan’s collapse as the specific moment at which Jinnah’s long-standing strategy of using the Pakistan demand as leverage for a strong, autonomous Muslim position within a loosely federated united India finally and irreversibly failed, making outright partition — which the League had previously used mainly as a negotiating threat rather than a fixed objective — the only remaining live option.
Direct Action Day (August 1946).

Following the collapse of the Cabinet Mission negotiations, the Muslim League called for a “Direct Action Day” on 16 August 1946 to press its demand for Pakistan, which triggered severe communal violence in Calcutta (often called the “Great Calcutta Killings”) and subsequently spread to other regions including Bihar and, later, Punjab. This violence marked a serious deterioration from constitutional negotiation toward large-scale communal conflict, and it forms an essential part of the context for understanding why the final transfer of power, discussed next, was accelerated and handled with what many historians regard as insufficient preparation for the human consequences involved.

blocks.text: Breakdown and the 3 June Plan: Partition and Independence

segments.text: By early 1947, several forces converged to make partition, previously one option among several, the only remaining practical path to a transfer of power: continuing and escalating communal violence, mounting British domestic and financial pressure to end the increasingly costly and difficult commitment in India, the appointment of Lord Mountbatten as the final Viceroy with an explicit mandate to arrange a transfer of power by June 1948 (a deadline he subsequently, controversially, moved forward), and the accumulated failure of every previous formula for a united, federally safeguarded India.
Mountbatten’s
3 June Plan

(1947) proposed partitioning British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, with the two Muslim-majority provinces of Punjab and Bengal themselves to be partitioned (rather than transferred whole to Pakistan), since each contained substantial non-Muslim-majority districts. Boundary Commissions, chaired by the British judge Sir Cyril Radcliffe, were tasked with drawing the actual dividing lines within an extremely compressed timeframe of only a few weeks, working from data on population, religion and other factors that were, in several contested areas, genuinely close and difficult to adjudicate fairly within the time allowed. The
Indian Independence Act 1947
, passed by the British Parliament, gave legal effect to this plan, and Pakistan and India became independent dominions on
14 and 15 August 1947
respectively.

The human consequences of the resulting partition of Punjab and Bengal were catastrophic and should not be treated as a mere administrative footnote to the constitutional narrative: an estimated ten to fifteen million people were displaced across the new borders in one of the largest mass migrations in human history, and communal violence during this migration killed what most careful historical estimates place at several hundred thousand to over a million people (precise figures remain genuinely disputed and are unlikely ever to be settled with certainty, given the chaos of the period and the absence of any single reliable contemporary count). Princely states, whose position had been left constitutionally unresolved by both the Cabinet Mission Plan and the 3 June Plan (since paramountcy over the princely states was to lapse with the transfer of power, leaving each state technically free to accede to either dominion or, in principle, remain independent), became an immediate and urgent problem the moment independence took effect — most acceded relatively smoothly, but a small number of contested cases, most importantly Jammu and Kashmir, produced disputes with consequences extending directly into Topic 10’s account of Pakistan’s foreign policy and security concerns.

items.text: Lahore Resolution (1940):
The Muslim League’s formal demand for autonomous, sovereign Muslim-majority “States,” conventionally regarded as the founding constitutional moment of the demand that became Pakistan.
Cabinet Mission Plan (1946):

The British proposal for a united India with a weak centre and grouped provinces, seeking Muslim safeguards without partition; its collapse over the compulsory-versus-optional grouping dispute is widely regarded as the point of no return.
3 June Plan (1947):
Mountbatten’s final plan partitioning British India into the dominions of India and Pakistan, including the partition of Punjab and Bengal themselves.
Radcliffe Line:
The boundary drawn by Sir Cyril Radcliffe’s Boundary Commissions dividing Punjab and Bengal between the two new dominions.
Paramountcy (lapse of):
The end, on independence, of the British Crown’s overarching authority over princely states, leaving each state to decide its own accession.

segments.text: This is one of the most consequential debates in all of South Asian history, and it connects directly to the Ayesha Jalal thesis introduced in Topic 4.

items.text: The “inevitability” reading

, more common in older nationalist historiography on both the Indian and Pakistani sides (though for different reasons), tends to treat the sequence from the Lahore Resolution (1940) to partition (1947) as the working-out of a demand that was, in substance, already settled by 1940.
Jalal’s “bargaining counter” reading

argues instead that Jinnah’s central and consistent strategy throughout the 1940s was to use the threat of partition to extract a strong, effectively autonomous position for Muslim-majority provinces within a loosely federated united India — and that the Cabinet Mission Plan’s collapse in 1946, specifically over the compulsory-versus-optional grouping dispute, is the moment this strategy demonstrably failed, making full partition, previously a fallback threat, the only remaining live option. On this reading, partition was a contingent outcome of a specific negotiation failure in 1946, not a fixed destination since 1940.
A related debate concerns British responsibility.

Some historians and much popular memory in the subcontinent has emphasised a “divide and quit” narrative, attributing partition significantly to deliberate British manipulation of communal division to facilitate an orderly, low-cost exit. Other historians place more emphasis on the structural failure of the Congress–League negotiations themselves (the compulsory-versus-optional grouping dispute, and the deeper disagreement over what “safeguards” for a minority within a democratic system could realistically mean), with British policy in the final months (particularly Mountbatten’s compressed timetable and Radcliffe’s rushed boundary-drawing) treated as a serious contributing failure of implementation rather than the primary underlying cause.

segments.text: A strong exam answer on “was partition inevitable?” should engage with the Cabinet Mission Plan specifically as the test case — since it is the one serious, detailed proposal that both major parties initially accepted and that would have avoided partition — and explain concretely why its collapse, rather than any single earlier moment, is where most careful historians locate the point after which partition became effectively unavoidable.
Preparation Checklist

items.text: Prepare a single 1930–1947 timeline. For every mission or plan, write down: the proposal, the League’s position, the Congress position, the British objective, and the specific reason for failure or success — the comparison table above is a model for this.
Treat the Lahore Resolution (1940) and the Cabinet Mission Plan’s collapse (1946) as the two most important turning points in the topic, and be ready to explain precisely why each mattered.

Keep an evidence bank: Allahabad Address (December 1930), Round Table Conferences (1930–1932), 1937 elections and Congress ministries (1937–1939), Lahore Resolution (March 1940), Cripps Mission (1942), Simla Conference (1945), 1945–46 elections, Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), Direct Action Day (August 1946), 3 June Plan (1947), independence (14–15 August 1947).
Practice one analytical outline answering: “Why did the Cabinet Mission Plan fail, and why is its failure often treated as the point after which partition became unavoidable?”

segments.text: Common Confusions to Avoid

items.text: Do not say the Pakistan demand appeared suddenly and fully formed in 1940; explain the earlier history of constitutional safeguards traced in Topic 4, and note that even after 1940 the League continued negotiating for safeguards within a united India until 1946.

Do not describe every pre-1947 Muslim political leader, or Jinnah himself at every stage, as advocating the identical territorial solution at the same time; positions evolved substantially between 1929, 1930, 1940 and 1946.
Do not study missions and plans only by date; for each one, know the proposal, League response, Congress response, British purpose, and the precise reason it failed or succeeded.

Do not treat the human cost of partition (mass migration and communal violence in Punjab and Bengal) as a separate topic from the constitutional negotiation; the two are directly connected, since the compressed timetable and rushed boundary-drawing of 1947 are themselves widely cited causes of the scale of the violence.

segments.text: Easy Revision Points

items.text: Iqbal delivered his Allahabad Address in December 1930, addressing the constitutional future of Muslim-majority north-western regions within the debate of that specific moment, not proposing a fully formed sovereign state.
The Round Table Conferences were held in London between 1930 and 1932.
Congress ministries governed several provinces after the 1937 elections and resigned in 1939 following the outbreak of the Second World War.
The Lahore Resolution was adopted by the Muslim League in March 1940; its original wording referred to “independent States,” plural, in Muslim-majority zones.

The Cripps Mission came in 1942, the Simla Conference was held in 1945, and the Cabinet Mission arrived in 1946; the Cabinet Mission Plan’s collapse over the compulsory-versus-optional grouping dispute is widely regarded as the point after which partition became effectively unavoidable.

The 3 June Plan of 1947 provided the framework for partition and transfer of power; Pakistan and India became independent dominions on 14 and 15 August 1947, at a human cost — mass displacement and communal violence — that remains historically significant in its own right.

The Muslim political demand moved from safeguards within a united India (Topic 4, through 1929) to a demand for separate, sovereign Muslim-majority “States” only at the 1940 Lahore Resolution, and even after 1940 the League continued to negotiate seriously for safeguards within a united India until as late as 1946.

The Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) is the pivotal case: it is the one detailed, serious proposal that both major parties initially accepted, and its collapse over the compulsory-versus-optional interpretation of provincial grouping is where most historians locate the point after which partition became effectively the only remaining option.

Every mission or plan in this period should be analysed from three angles at once — League objective, Congress objective, British objective — since no single-party explanation for any mission’s failure survives close examination.

The human cost of partition (mass migration and communal violence in Punjab and Bengal) is directly connected to, not separate from, the compressed and rushed final negotiation and boundary-drawing process of 1947, and deserves serious treatment rather than a footnote.

Whether partition was “inevitable” remains a genuinely open historiographical question; Ayesha Jalal’s influential argument that it resulted from the specific failure of a bargaining strategy in 1946, rather than being fixed since 1940, is worth citing explicitly in any strong answer on this question.
